title: Rafael and the Letters
premise: Marine biologist Mirabel Okonkwo has spent a decade training her heart like any other muscle: contained, measurable, safe. When her sister's wedding forces her home to Lagos, she hires Rafael Adeyemi — a struggling baker and old classmate — to pose as her boyfriend for one weekend. But the fake date turns real by dessert, and a box of unsent letters Rafael wrote ten years ago reveals he was the boy who once loved her and vanished without explanation. As the bakery lease deadline looms, Mirabel must decide whether loyalty to her own survival rules matters more than the truth: that Rafael left because her family paid him to, and that loving him was never something she could train away. The story ends with Rafael reading his final letter aloud in the bakery on its last night of business, and Mirabel answering with the sentence she has rehearsed for a decade.
about_author: Theo Yarrow is the pen name of a former marine science communicator turned novelist who writes love stories set against coastlines and family obligations. They live between two cities and believe every good romance begins with someone lying to themselves.

chapters.title: Counting Turtles
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. On a research boat off the Atlantic, Mirabel logs turtle nests with clinical precision while dodging her mother's calls about the wedding invitation. Her colleague teases that she catalogs everything except her feelings. Emotional beat: controlled loneliness disguised as discipline.

chapters.title: The Invitation
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. The wedding invitation arrives with a handwritten note from her mother: 'Bring someone real this time.' Flashback fragments hint at a boy from her past she refuses to name. She drafts a plan to hire a date. Emotional beat: dread wrapped in competence.

chapters.title: Flour and Salt
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. In his failing bakery, Rafael counts the days left on his lease — eleven weeks. A familiar face walks in: Mirabel Okonkwo, the girl he loved at nineteen. He plays it cool; his hands shake kneading dough. Emotional beat: hope arriving dressed as trouble.

chapters.title: Terms and Conditions
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. Over burnt plantain bread, Mirabel proposes the arrangement: one weekend, one wedding, payment generous enough to save the bakery. Rafael hesitates, then agrees — for reasons he doesn't say aloud. Emotional beat: a contract built on mutual avoidance.

chapters.title: Rehearsal
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. They rehearse their 'how we met' story in the empty bakery after hours, laughing until the laughter stops feeling performed. Rafael almost tells her something true; a customer interrupts. Emotional beat: the first crack in the performance.

chapters.title: Arrival
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. They drive to the family compound in Enugu, hands linked for the cameras of aunties. Her mother studies Rafael too long. Her sister Chiamaka pulls Mirabel aside: 'Him? Really?' Emotional beat: the past pressing against the present like weather.

chapters.title: The First Dinner
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. At dinner, Mirabel's father interrogates Rafael about his bakery's finances. Rafael answers honestly about struggle, which surprises everyone — including himself. Mirabel squeezes his knee under the table. Emotional beat: unexpected solidarity.

chapters.title: Dessert
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. On the veranda after dessert, they slip away from the party and almost kiss — stopped by Chiamaka calling Mirabel's name. Walking back separately, both admit internally that the act has stopped being an act. Emotional beat: the point of no return, unspoken.

chapters.title: The Wedding
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. The wedding is beautiful and suffocating. During the vows, Rafael watches Mirabel instead of the couple. An elderly aunt mistakes them for engaged; neither corrects her fast enough. Emotional beat: envy of a love declared publicly.

chapters.title: Letters, Part One
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. Packing up at the compound, Mirabel finds a letter in Rafael's jacket pocket — dated ten years ago, addressed to her, never sent. It stops mid-sentence. She pockets it without telling him. Emotional beat: betrayal by curiosity.

chapters.title: What He Didn't Say
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. Back in Lagos, Rafael senses Mirabel pulling away but can't ask why. His landlord serves formal notice: the lease ends in six weeks. He begins writing a new letter he'll probably never send. Emotional beat: running out of time twice over.

chapters.title: The Second Letter
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. Mirabel returns to the bakery under a pretext and finds a shoebox of letters — one per year, all to her, all unsent. The earliest explains nothing; it only apologizes. She leaves before he sees her. Emotional beat: grief for a decade misread.

chapters.title: Confrontation at Closing Time
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Mirabel confronts Rafael with the letters. He admits he wrote them but refuses to explain why he disappeared. 'You wouldn't want the truth,' he says. She throws the contract money on the counter. Emotional beat: anger as armor.

chapters.title: Chiamaka's Version
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. Chiamaka visits and, seeing Mirabel unraveling, confesses what she knows: ten years ago, their father paid Rafael's family to send him abroad and keep him away — because Mirabel was 'too young, too promising.' Emotional beat: the ground shifting beneath loyalty.

chapters.title: The Price of Survival
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. Rafael's flashback chapter: nineteen years old, a father's medical debt, an envelope of cash, and a promise extracted — never contact her. He took the money to keep his family alive and has been paying interest ever since. Emotional beat: shame finally given context.

chapters.title: Silence Between Shifts
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. Three weeks pass. Mirabel throws herself into work, but the turtle data blurs — she can't count anything anymore. Her mother, unexpectedly gentle, says: 'We protected you into a smaller life than you deserved.' Emotional beat: inherited guilt examined.

chapters.title: Lease Expiry
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. The final week of the bakery. Rafael boxes up ovens and memories, keeping only the shoebox. Chiamaka appears at the counter and tells him Mirabel knows everything — and came back to the bakery three times while he wasn't there. Emotional beat: a door reopening at closing time.

chapters.title: The Last Night
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. On the bakery's final night, Rafael lights the ovens one last time and bakes the plantain bread from their first meeting. He writes letter number eleven — the first he intends to deliver. Emotional beat: courage assembled from ruins.

chapters.title: Read Aloud
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. Mirabel arrives, having followed the smell of baking through the rain. Rafael reads the new letter aloud: the truth of the money, the years of silence, and the sentence he rehearsed for a decade — that he never stopped loving her. Emotional beat: vulnerability as climax.

chapters.title: The Rehearsed Sentence
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. Mirabel finally speaks the sentence she has practiced alone for ten years — not blame, but the confession that she waited, counted turtles to avoid counting days, and loves him still. They kiss amid flour dust and cooling racks. Emotional beat: release.

chapters.title: New Lease
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Epilogue-adjacent: Rafael's father offers restitution; Mirabel negotiates peace with her father on her own terms. Together they find a smaller storefront with a bigger window. Emotional beat: rebuilding without erasing the cost.

chapters.title: What the Tide Brings Back
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV, one year later. The new bakery opens above her research station; the letters are framed behind the counter, all eleven finally delivered. A turtle she once tagged returns to nest. Emotional beat: the heart, trained at last, chooses freely.
